title: Oregon Blew Up a Dead Whale. It Rained Blubber. #shorts
description:
Case 041. On 12 November 1970 a dead whale, about 45 feet long and some 8 tons, lay on the beach at Florence, Oregon. The Oregon State Highway Division, with assistant district engineer George Thornton in charge, packed twenty 50-pound cases of dynamite (half a ton) against it, expecting the blast to leave pieces small enough for seagulls and other scavengers to clean up. Spectators were moved back into the dunes. Walter Umenhofer, who had explosives training from his war service, said it was far too much and watched from further back than the rest of the crowd. The blast threw a column of sand and whale into the air; blubber sailed over the spectators and people ran for their cars. About a quarter of a mile away, a slab of blubber crushed the roof of the new car Umenhofer had bought days earlier in a "whale of a deal" sales promotion; the state's insurer paid him the car's full value. Nobody was hit. Highway crews cleaned up what was left, and Thornton told the local paper it "went just exactly right". In 2020 the people of Florence voted to name a new park Exploding Whale Memorial Park. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The whale was already dead; nobody was hurt. The cars, cases, bulldozer and dealer's forecourt are generic low-poly shapes with no makes, logos or brand names, and nobody's likeness is attempted. The only words on screen are the documented sales slogan and the park's name. Staging details such as the look of the beach, the crates, the car, the dealer's forecourt, the park and the sign, who stood where, and everything Rook does are reconstruction, not record. Narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro).
